answer.label: Not Mencken's wording — a padded version of a real 1920 line
answer.sourceLine: Mencken really did make this prophecy, in “Bayard vs. Lionheart,” The Evening Sun (Baltimore), 26 July 1920 — but he wrote that the White House would one day be “adorned by a downright moron,” not “occupied by a downright fool and a complete narcissistic moron.” Snopes ↗, which quotes the padded version word for word, states plainly that Mencken’s original made no mention of fools or narcissism. The idea is his; this exact sentence is not.

source.heading: What the 1920 column actually says

docMeta.dd: “… the White House will be adorned by a downright moron.”

source.excerpt: All the odds are on the man who is, intrinsically, the most devious and mediocre — the man who can most adeptly disperse the notion that his mind is a virtual vacuum. The Presidency tends, year by year, to go to such men. As democracy is perfected, the office represents, more and more closely, the inner soul of the people. We move toward a lofty ideal. On some great and glorious day the plain folks of the land will reach their heart’s desire at last, and the White House will be adorned by a downright moron.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ cites The Evening Sun (Baltimore) of 26 July 1920, page 8, column 5, article “Bayard vs. Lionheart” by H. L. Mencken, and reproduces the passage ending “adorned by a downright moron.” It also records the column’s reprinting in A Carnival of Buncombe (Johns Hopkins Press, 1956).
The sourced section of Wikiquote ↗ carries the identical wording — “the office represents” and “adorned by a downright moron” — under the same 26 July 1920 citation.

Snopes ↗ rates the attribution “Correct Attribution,” quotes the padded “fool and a complete narcissistic moron” version in full, and adds that Mencken’s original statement made no mention of fools or narcissism.
WIST Quotations ↗ lists the same padded text explicitly under “Variant,” kept separate from the sourced 1920 sentence.
source.excerptNote: This is the passage as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ and by the sourced section of Wikiquote ↗. Set against the viral text, three differences stand out: “the office” rather than “the office of the President,” the retained sentence “We move toward a lofty ideal,” and “adorned by a downright moron” rather than “occupied by a downright fool and a complete narcissistic moron.”

source.rightsNote: The work quoted here — Mencken’s column “Bayard vs. Lionheart,” first published in The Evening Sun (Baltimore) on 26 July 1920 — appeared in the United States well before 1931 and is in the public domain. The extra words in the circulating version (“a downright fool and a complete narcissistic moron”) have no identifiable author or publication of their own; they are an anonymous later alteration rather than text from any Mencken work, and nothing here should be read as a rights claim over them. The 1956 A Carnival of Buncombe collection is a separate, later publication.

author.name: H. L. Mencken
author.heading: The man who actually wrote it
author.bio: Henry Louis Mencken was born in Baltimore on 12 September 1880 and died there on 29 January 1956, having spent most of his working life at the Sun papers, including The Evening Sun, where this column ran. In 1924 he and George Jean Nathan founded and edited The American Mercury, which he left as editor in 1933; his other major work includes The American Language (1919) and the six-series Prejudices. His register — contemptuous, comic and endlessly quotable — is exactly why people keep improving his sentences for him.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong words
misattribution.intro: This is the rarer kind of quotation problem: the name on it is correct, and the sentence still is not what he wrote. Three separate edits separate the viral text from the 1920 column.

items.who: “a downright fool and a complete narcissistic moron”
items.why: Mencken wrote that the White House would be “adorned by a downright moron.” Snopes ↗ prints the padded wording and notes that Mencken’s original statement made no mention of fools or narcissism. The added “narcissistic” was already being flagged as an alteration in January 2017 ↗.
Both Quote Investigator ↗ and the sourced entry at Wikiquote ↗ transcribe “adorned by a downright moron” from the 1920 column. “Occupied” loses the sarcasm of a moron as ornament.

items.who: “the office of the President” — and the missing sentence
items.why: The 1920 text reads simply “the office represents,” and follows it with “We move toward a lofty ideal,” which the popular version drops entirely. Compare the full passage at Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The real story: a genuine Mencken prophecy from “Bayard vs. Lionheart,” The Evening Sun (Baltimore), 26 July 1920 ↗ — sharpened by anonymous hands somewhere between the 2004 blogs and the 2017 memes.

context.heading: Why Mencken was in this mood
lead: Mencken wrote the column in the summer of 1920, sizing up a presidential contest between Warren G. Harding and James M. Cox that he regarded as a choice between two nonentities — the Baltimore Sun ↗ notes he had no respect for either man. His argument was mechanical rather than merely rude: the bigger the electorate, the more a campaign has to be waged at second and third hand, and the more the odds favour the candidate who can best conceal an empty mind.

The line then lay quiet for decades. Snopes ↗ records it gaining currency on political blogs at the end of 2004, aimed at George W. Bush, then being redeployed against Barack Obama and later Donald Trump. Somewhere in that relay the sentence picked up its extra insults — a quotation sharpened to fit whoever it was being thrown at.
context.detailsSummary: What the padded version gains, and loses
detailsBody: The edits are not neutral. “Adorned” is a sneer — Mencken is picturing the moron as decoration, the nation’s taste made visible. “Occupied” flattens that into a statement of tenancy.

The padded version also drops “We move toward a lofty ideal,” the deadpan half-sentence that makes the passage satire rather than abuse. It is a fair rule of thumb for altered quotations: the additions usually raise the volume and lower the wit.
